title: "Assignment B — Computational comparison of gradient methods"
subtitle: "Accuracy, sample size, momentum costs and repeated-dose compression"

# A shared numerical and computational study

This report uses the same `study_settings()`, `run_study()` and geometry experiment
as the [simulation report](dose_response_simulation.html). Starts, data, seeds and
controls match; timings are fresh measurements. Newton is excluded. Multi-start
BFGS is used only for a best-found numerical reference, not as a timed competitor.

Compare full-gradient GD, Polyak and Nesterov with safeguarded Armijo searches;
full-gradient GD with power-law decay; mini-batch SGD, Polyak and Nesterov
with that decay; and mini-batch AdaGrad with a fixed base rate. These are
comparisons of implementations and step policies under shared, non-optimal tuning.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("project_B/model.R")
source("project_B/data.R")
source("project_B/solvers.R")
source("project_B/experiments.R")
source("project_B/plots.R")
library(ggplot2)
# Match the current simulation QMD override. Edit this in both reports together.
settings <- study_settings()
settings$batch_size <- 16
results <- run_study(settings)
comparison <- study_summary(results, settings)
large <- results[["grid_15000"]]$dataset$problem
theta <- results[["grid_15000"]]$start
```

# Accuracy against time

The stochastic budget is `r settings$epochs` epochs with batch size
`r settings$batch_size` and initial rate `r settings$gamma0`.
Scheduled rates use exponent `r settings$a` and half-time `r settings$half_epochs`
epochs; AdaGrad keeps its base rate fixed. Momentum is 0.9. Armijo methods share trial step 1, c = 0.0001, halving,
at most 2,000 updates, and gradient infinity-norm tolerance 1e-8.

Equal epochs are equal passes, not equal updates. Full-batch scheduled GD takes 15
updates; mini-batch SGD takes $15\lceil N/b\rceil$. Armijo methods may use additional passes
for line search. Report accuracy against wall time and first recorded time within
0.0001 MSE of the best-found reference. NA means no recorded attainment within
budget. First attainment does not imply sustained accuracy. This is not a global
optimality certificate; negative reference differences would prompt further search.

Full-MSE monitoring is included in traces, every quarter epoch where possible.
Full-batch scheduled GD can record only once per epoch. Data generation and reference
search are excluded. Execute benchmarks sequentially to avoid CPU contention.

```{r}
#| label: main-summary
main_rows <- comparison[!startsWith(comparison$run, "grouped_"), ]
knitr::kable(main_rows[, c("design", "N", "method", "seed", "status", "updates", "objective",
                         "seconds", "seconds_to_target", "restarts")],
             digits = 6, row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: main-convergence
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 10
plot_study(results)
```

```{r}
#| label: small-detail
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 6
plot_study(results[c("grid_300", "continuous_300")])
```

Each panel has its own time scale and a shared MSE scale. Compare the numerical
time-axis labels, not horizontal distances across panels. The small-sample view
provides more space for inspecting those trajectories. These are two shuffle replicates on fixed datasets, not repeated
simulations establishing a universal ranking. Short times have limited clock resolution.

# Which method reaches the requested accuracy first?

An algorithm can be useful at a loose accuracy requirement but become expensive at
a strict one. The following heatmap compares three requirements on the **same**
recorded trajectories. Each cell labels how many runs reached the threshold; its
color shows the median first-attainment time among those runs. Grey means no
attainment within budget, not that the method would never reach the target.
A 1/2 cell is not directly comparable in reliability to a 2/2 cell. Deterministic
methods have one run, so 1/1 is not evidence of robustness over datasets.

```{r}
#| label: accuracy-target-map
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 9
targets <- accuracy_targets(results)
plot_accuracy_targets(targets)
```

Read this with the final-error tables: an oscillating stochastic method may cross a
target briefly and then finish above it. These are first **recorded** crossings;
checkpoint spacing and millisecond timer resolution limit precision. The reference
is best-found, not a proven lower bound. Thus the target measures closeness to a
numerical reference, not a certified global optimization error.

This directly addresses the trade-off: noisy inexpensive updates may provide a
useful approximation quickly, whereas full-gradient methods can offer steadier
refinement. Whether that happens here is determined by the colored cells and
attainment labels, not assumed from the algorithm names.

# Cost per update versus number of updates

With p = 4 parameters, an individual gradient costs O(p), a full gradient O(Np),
and a full objective O(N). An epoch of single-observation updates costs O(Np),
plus shuffling and monitoring. A full-gradient update is more expensive but can
make more reliable progress. Vectorized R evaluation also avoids the repeated
function calls and small allocations in a single-observation loop.

Polyak stores a p-vector and adds O(p) work per update. Nesterov uses a look-ahead
gradient; our deterministic version also checks the current gradient for stopping
and may restart. AdaGrad stores p squared-gradient accumulators and adapts coordinates
in O(p). Backtracking costs extra objective evaluations. These costs must be considered
alongside the number of updates needed to obtain an adequate fit.

```{r}
#| label: line-search-work
work <- data.frame()
for (name in names(results)) {
  for (method in c("full_gd", "full_polyak", "full_nesterov")) {
    fit <- results[[name]]$fits[[method]]
    work <- rbind(work, data.frame(case = name, method = fit$method,
      updates = tail(fit$history$update, 1), restarts = fit$restarts,
      objective_evaluations = fit$objective_evaluations,
      gradient_evaluations = fit$gradient_evaluations))
  }
}
knitr::kable(work, row.names = FALSE)
```

Objective counts include initialization, line-search trials and Nesterov look-ahead
checks. Gradient counts cover current and look-ahead gradients within the optimization
loop. The final stationarity check and summary calculations are outside these loop
counts. Restarts are part of the cost. The simulation report separately varies the
trial step while keeping Armijo c fixed.

# Batch size: speed, final error and progress per pass

Use the large grid and continuous datasets already fitted above, with batch sizes
1, 16, 64 and 256. Compare all four stochastic methods using the same starts,
seeds, initial rate, momentum and 15-epoch budget. Only batch size changes. The final
partial batch is averaged over its actual size. The settings below are editable.
This is an equal-pass experiment, not an equal-update or equal-time experiment.

```{r}
#| label: batch-study
batch_sizes <- c(1, 16, 64, 256)
batch_results <- run_batch_study(
  results[c("grid_15000", "continuous_15000")], settings, batches = batch_sizes
)
knitr::kable(batch_results$summary[, c("case", "method", "seed", "batch", "status",
  "updates", "objective", "difference_from_reference", "seconds", "seconds_to_target")],
  digits = 6, row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: batch-tradeoff
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 11
plot_batch_tradeoff(batch_results, accuracy = settings$accuracy)
```

Each point is one run. Lower-left means a smaller final error in less total time.
Filled points indicate that the target was reached at least once, not necessarily
maintained. Signed differences remain in the table; the log plot uses a display
floor of 1e-8. Both seeds are shown even if their points overlap.

Now compare progress per pass through the observations, removing wall-clock speed
from the horizontal axis. This distinguishes an implementation saving from more
progress for the same amount of data processed.

```{r}
#| label: batch-passes
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 11
traces <- batch_results$traces
ggplot(traces, aes(passes, pmax(reference_difference, 1e-8),
                  color = factor(batch), group = interaction(batch, seed))) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = settings$accuracy, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_grid(method ~ case) + scale_y_log10() + theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(x = "Passes through the observations", color = "Batch size",
       y = "MSE minus reference (display floor: 1e-8)")
```

Increasing b makes each gradient more expensive, but reduces the number of R calls
and updates per epoch to approximately N/b. It usually reduces sampling noise at a
fixed parameter, but fewer updates can leave more error after 15 passes. The decay
schedule still changes by epoch, so larger batches get fewer updates before each
rate reduction. AdaGrad also accumulates a different gradient history.

The best batch size therefore depends on the method, accuracy requirement and
implementation. Because the rates are held fixed, this experiment measures
sensitivity rather than the best possible performance of every batch size.
The stochastic runs use original observations; grid grouping is a separate exact
full-gradient shortcut examined below.

# Local geometry changes the required effort

Repeat the simulation report's slopes 0.35, 1.2 and 4 on the same 1,500 continuous
doses and noise realization. Keep plateaus, center, common start and controls fixed.
Each evaluation has similar cost, while progress can differ because the geometry
and distance from the shared start change.

```{r}
#| label: geometry-cost
#| results: asis
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
geometry_results <- run_sensitivity(settings, "geometry")
knitr::kable(geometry_summary(geometry_results), digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
for (name in names(geometry_results)) {
  case <- geometry_results[[name]]
  print(knitr::kable(fit_summary(case$fits, case$dataset$problem, case$reference),
                     digits = 6, row.names = FALSE, caption = name))
  print(plot_convergence(case$fits, case$reference) + ggtitle(name))
}
```

The exact Hessian ratio is reported only when positive definite; the Jacobian
curvature ratio is a positive-semidefinite diagnostic. Both are local and depend
on parameter units. Neither establishes global strong convexity. See the fitted
curves in the simulation report for the consequences of remaining optimization error.

# Exploit repeated doses without changing the objective

For each distinct dose retain its count $n_j$, response mean $\bar y_j$ and
within-dose sum of squares $S_j$. Then
$$H(\theta)=\frac1N\sum_j[S_j+n_j(\bar y_j-f(x_j;\theta))^2].$$
The cross term vanishes because deviations from a group mean sum to zero. The
within-dose term is parameter-independent but retained for comparable MSE values.
Gradients require only weighted dose means.

For a known 15-point grid, summaries can be accumulated in one pass; subsequent
evaluations depend on 15 groups rather than N. The generic helper also identifies
and orders distinct doses, so we measure preprocessing. Grouping is exact, not
rounding or binning. Continuous doses are almost surely distinct and offer no useful
compression. Full-gradient momentum can use the same exact summaries. Stochastic
methods keep the original observations: replacing individual responses by means
would change their updates and noise.

```{r}
#| label: grouping-check
preprocessing <- system.time(grouped <- group_doses(large))[["elapsed"]]
data.frame(N = large$N, groups = length(grouped$z), preprocessing_seconds = preprocessing)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(objective(theta, large), objective(theta, grouped))))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(gradient(theta, large), gradient(theta, grouped))))
```

```{r}
#| label: grouped-results
grid_rows <- comparison[comparison$design == "grid" &
                         (startsWith(comparison$run, "grouped_") |
                          comparison$run %in% c("full_gd", "full_polyak", "full_nesterov")), ]
knitr::kable(grid_rows[, c("N", "method", "status", "objective", "seconds",
                         "seconds_to_target", "restarts")], digits = 6, row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: grouped-convergence
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 8
plot_study(results[c("grid_300", "grid_15000")], include_grouped = TRUE)
```

Each grouped trace includes preprocessing. Starts and controls match, and summaries
are evaluated against the original observations. Floating-point summation can change
a line-search decision near a threshold; the mathematical problem is identical.
A speedup exploits data structure, not different statistical accuracy or convexity.

# Repeated benchmarks

Equivalent kernel benchmarks retain equality checking. They exclude preprocessing;
the end-to-end comparisons below include it every time. Memory allocation is not
peak resident memory.

```{r}
#| label: kernels
bench::mark(raw = objective(theta, large), grouped = objective(theta, grouped),
             check = TRUE, min_iterations = 30)
bench::mark(raw = gradient(theta, large), grouped = gradient(theta, grouped),
             check = TRUE, min_iterations = 30)
```

```{r}
#| label: scaling
scaling <- data.frame()
for (name in c("grid_300", "grid_15000")) {
  case <- results[[name]]
  p <- case$dataset$problem
  start <- case$start
  compressed <- group_doses(p)
  timings <- bench::mark(
    raw_gradient = gradient(start, p),
    grouped_gradient = gradient(start, compressed),
    grouping = group_doses(p), check = FALSE, min_iterations = 30)
  scaling <- rbind(scaling, data.frame(N = p$N,
    operation = as.character(timings$expression), seconds = as.numeric(timings$median),
    bytes = as.numeric(timings$mem_alloc)))
}
knitr::kable(scaling, digits = 7, row.names = FALSE)
ggplot(scaling, aes(N, seconds, color = operation)) + geom_line() + geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() + theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Number of observations", y = "Median seconds per operation")
```

Only the mixed benchmark disables checking because a grouped data object is not a
gradient. Equality is verified separately. Complete solver benchmarks include garbage
collection: allocation costs are part of performance.

```{r}
#| label: end-to-end
solver_samples <- data.frame()
for (name in c("grid_300", "grid_15000")) {
  case <- results[[name]]
  p <- case$dataset$problem
  start <- case$start
  for (method in c("full_gd", "full_polyak", "full_nesterov")) {
    cat(name, method, "\n")
    timings <- bench::mark(
      raw = {
        fit <- study_fit(p, method, start, settings)
        objective(fit$theta, p)
      },
      grouped = {
        compressed <- group_doses(p)
        fit <- study_fit(compressed, method, start, settings)
        objective(fit$theta, p)
      },
      check = TRUE, iterations = 5, filter_gc = FALSE
    )
    print(timings)
    samples <- benchmark_samples(timings)
    samples$case <- name
    samples$method <- unname(method_labels()[method])
    solver_samples <- rbind(solver_samples, samples)
  }
}
```

Both expressions return the final original-data MSE. Five repetitions are illustrative;
use more for precise estimates. If equality fails, investigate numerical paths rather
than silently disabling the check. Consult the accuracy table before treating a
shorter budget-exhausted run as a faster solution.

## Distribution of complete solver timings

The beeswarm shows every timed repetition, including garbage collection. Black
bars mark medians. Grouped timings include preprocessing on every repetition.
These repeated durations measure system variability for the same computation;
they are not independent simulated datasets or shuffle seeds.

```{r}
#| label: solver-beeswarm
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 9
ggplot(solver_samples, aes(implementation, seconds, color = implementation)) +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_quasirandom(width = 0.2, size = 2) +
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "point", shape = 95, size = 8, color = "black") +
  facet_grid(method ~ case) + scale_y_log10() + theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Seconds per complete fit (log scale)")
```

# Profile the loop at different batch sizes

Profile plain SGD at batches 1, 16 and 256 using the same large grid data. Repeat
each calculation for at least one second of profiling so a very short batched run
still yields enough samples. Each repetition resets the same seed. Profiling is
separate from the timing experiments because instrumentation adds overhead.

```{r}
#| label: profiling
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 8
profile_rows <- data.frame()
for (batch in c(1, 16, 256)) {
  controls <- settings
  controls$batch_size <- batch
  profile_file <- tempfile()
  started <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
  Rprof(profile_file, interval = 0.001)
  tryCatch({
    repeat {
      invisible(study_fit(large, "sgd", theta, controls, seed = 201))
      if (proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - started >= 1) break
    }
  }, finally = Rprof(NULL))
  profile <- summaryRprof(profile_file)
  top <- head(profile$by.self, 10)
  profile_rows <- rbind(profile_rows, data.frame(batch = batch,
    function_name = gsub('"', '', rownames(top)), self_percent = top$self.pct))
  unlink(profile_file)
}
ggplot(profile_rows, aes(self_percent, reorder(function_name, self_percent))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#4477AA") + facet_wrap(~batch, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  theme_minimal() + labs(x = "Percent of sampled time spent directly in function",
                         y = NULL, subtitle = "Top 10 self-time contributors; panels show batch size")
```

Self time excludes callees, avoiding the double-counting that would occur if nested
total times were added together. The top ten functions need not sum to 100 percent.
These are sampled proportions, not repeated timing distributions, so a bar plot is
more appropriate here than a beeswarm. Inspect how gradient construction, loop
work, allocations and monitoring change with batch size. Small gradients may be
cheap individually yet expensive when called hundreds of thousands of times.

```{r}
#| eval: false
profvis::profvis(study_fit(large, "sgd", theta, settings, seed = 201))
```

## Check the cost of monitoring

Clock calls can appear prominently in the profile when updates are cheap. The
profile includes a small amount of timing in the repetition wrapper as well as
inside the solver, so use this separate benchmark to assess actual monitoring cost.
At batch size 256, change only recording frequency: every quarter epoch, every
epoch or every five epochs. Each run still performs the same updates with the same
seed. Equality checking compares the **final parameter vectors**, not just rounded
losses. Reduced monitoring makes target-attainment times less precisely observed,
so it is not a free improvement to the main accuracy comparison.

```{r}
#| label: monitoring-cost
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
quarter <- settings
quarter$batch_size <- 256
quarter$monitor_epochs <- 0.25
every_epoch <- quarter
every_epoch$monitor_epochs <- 1
every_five <- quarter
every_five$monitor_epochs <- 5
monitor_timings <- bench::mark(
  quarter_epoch = study_fit(large, "sgd", theta, quarter, seed = 201)$theta,
  every_epoch = study_fit(large, "sgd", theta, every_epoch, seed = 201)$theta,
  every_five_epochs = study_fit(large, "sgd", theta, every_five, seed = 201)$theta,
  check = TRUE, iterations = 10, filter_gc = FALSE
)
monitor_timings
monitor_samples <- benchmark_samples(monitor_timings)
ggplot(monitor_samples, aes(implementation, seconds * 1000, color = implementation)) +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_quasirandom(width = 0.2, size = 2) +
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "point", shape = 95, size = 8, color = "black") +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(x = "Recording frequency", y = "Milliseconds per complete SGD run")
```

# R versus Rcpp: timing distributions and allocation

C++ accumulates four derivatives directly instead of constructing a response-gradient
matrix. Benchmark batches 1, 16, 64, 256 and full N, using identical precomputed
indices for R and C++. Equality checking stays enabled. Compilation and sampling
are excluded. Each beeswarm contains 200 repeated evaluations, including GC events.

```{r}
#| label: cpp
Rcpp::sourceCpp("project_B/gradient.cpp")
cpp_samples <- data.frame()
cpp_summary <- data.frame()
for (batch in c(1, 16, 64, 256, large$N)) {
  index <- seq_len(batch)
  timings <- bench::mark(R = gradient(theta, large, index),
    Rcpp = dose_gradient_cpp(theta, large$z, large$y, index),
    check = TRUE, iterations = 200, filter_gc = FALSE)
  samples <- benchmark_samples(timings)
  samples$batch <- batch
  cpp_samples <- rbind(cpp_samples, samples)
  cpp_summary <- rbind(cpp_summary, data.frame(batch = batch,
    implementation = as.character(timings$expression),
    median_seconds = as.numeric(timings$median), bytes = as.numeric(timings$mem_alloc)))
}
knitr::kable(cpp_summary, digits = 8, row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: cpp-beeswarm
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 7
ggplot(cpp_samples, aes(implementation, seconds * 1e6, color = implementation)) +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_quasirandom(width = 0.25, alpha = 0.45, size = 1.3) +
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "point", shape = 95, size = 8, color = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~batch, ncol = 3) + scale_y_log10() + theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Microseconds per gradient (log scale)",
       subtitle = "Panels: batch size. Points: repetitions. Black bar: median.")
```

```{r}
#| label: cpp-allocation
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
ggplot(cpp_summary, aes(factor(batch), bytes / 1024, fill = implementation)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") + theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Batch size", y = "R-tracked allocation per evaluation (KiB)")
```

Allocation is not peak memory, and R's tracker does not capture every possible
native C++ allocation. Retain the numeric table when small bars are hard to see.
The optimizer comparison still uses R gradients: these plots establish a kernel
speedup, not an end-to-end optimizer speedup. Use the profile to judge whether
accelerating gradients addresses a major cost. If a fraction f of runtime could
be accelerated by a factor s, an idealized total speedup is at most
$1/[(1-f)+f/s]$, assuming the rest of the computation is unchanged. Moving the
whole epoch loop into C++ addresses additional overhead; the next experiment tests this directly.

# Complete SGD loop: allocation and runtime

Here we compare complete mini-batch SGD update loops in R and C++, at batch sizes
1, 16, 64 and 256. Change `sgd_batch_sizes` below to choose other sizes.
Both process the same precomputed permutations with the same start and epoch-based
power-law rates. This isolates implementation costs: data generation, compilation,
permutation generation and trajectory monitoring are excluded from both timings.
These are complete update runs, not end-to-end timings of the report's monitored
solver. The other optimizer comparisons above remain unchanged.

```{r}
#| label: complete-sgd
# A simple R baseline: the same gradient and update used by plain SGD.
# No history is recorded, matching the C++ function's work.
dose_sgd_r <- function(start, problem, orders, rates, batch_size = 1L) {
  stopifnot(batch_size >= 1, batch_size <= problem$N, batch_size %% 1 == 0)
  theta <- start
  batch_starts <- seq.int(1L, nrow(orders), by = batch_size)
  for (epoch in seq_len(ncol(orders))) {
    for (first in batch_starts) {
      last <- min(first + batch_size - 1L, nrow(orders))
      index <- orders[first:last, epoch]
      # gradient() averages over the actual batch, even if the last is shorter.
      theta <- theta - rates[epoch] * gradient(theta, problem, index)
    }
  }
  theta
}
sgd_batch_sizes <- c(1L, 16L, 64L, 256L)

loop_samples <- data.frame()
loop_summary <- data.frame()
for (N in c(300, 15000)) {
  p <- simulate_doses(N, "continuous", seed = 2026)$problem
  start <- initial_parameters(p)
  epochs <- 15L
  set.seed(201)
  orders <- replicate(epochs, sample.int(N))
  rates <- learning_rate(0:(epochs - 1), settings$gamma0,
                         settings$half_epochs, settings$a)

  for (batch in sgd_batch_sizes) {
    # Compare both implementations at every batch size, before benchmarking.
    r_theta <- dose_sgd_r(start, p, orders, rates, batch)
    cpp_theta <- dose_sgd_cpp(start, p$z, p$y, orders, rates, batch)
    stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(r_theta, cpp_theta, tolerance = 1e-8)))
    timings <- bench::mark(
      R = dose_sgd_r(start, p, orders, rates, batch),
      Rcpp = dose_sgd_cpp(start, p$z, p$y, orders, rates, batch),
      iterations = 5, check = TRUE, filter_gc = FALSE)
    samples <- benchmark_samples(timings)
    samples$N <- N
    samples$batch <- batch
    loop_samples <- rbind(loop_samples, samples)
    loop_summary <- rbind(loop_summary, data.frame(
      N = N, batch = batch, implementation = as.character(timings$expression),
      median_seconds = as.numeric(timings$median),
      bytes = as.numeric(timings$mem_alloc),
      final_mse = c(objective(r_theta, p), objective(cpp_theta, p))))
  }
}
# A recorded zero is a measurement limitation, not zero memory use.
loop_summary$allocation <- ifelse(loop_summary$bytes == 0,
  "No allocation recorded", paste(format(round(loop_summary$bytes / 1024, 2),
  trim = TRUE), "KiB"))
knitr::kable(loop_summary[, c("N", "batch", "implementation", "median_seconds",
                            "allocation", "final_mse")], digits = 6)
```

```{r}
#| label: complete-sgd-time
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
ggplot(loop_samples, aes(factor(batch), seconds, color = implementation)) +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_quasirandom(width = 0.15, dodge.width = 0.6, size = 2) +
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "point", shape = 95, size = 8,
               color = "black", position = position_dodge(width = 0.6),
               aes(group = interaction(batch, implementation))) +
  facet_wrap(~N) + scale_y_log10() + theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(x = "Batch size", y = "Seconds per 15-epoch update run (log scale)",
       subtitle = "Same observations, ordering, rates and starting parameters")
```

## Recorded allocation across batch sizes

Each point represents cumulative R-tracked allocation for a complete 15-epoch run,
not allocation per update or peak memory. Larger batches create larger temporary
objects in R, but also require fewer updates. There is therefore no requirement for
cumulative allocation to increase monotonically with batch size.

```{r}
#| label: sgd-batch-allocation
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
# Plot only positive measurements on the log axis. Label unrecorded measurements
# in a separate table; never replace zero with a made-up positive allocation.
recorded <- loop_summary[loop_summary$bytes > 0, ]
unrecorded <- loop_summary[loop_summary$bytes == 0, ]
allocation_plot <- ggplot(recorded,
  aes(factor(batch), bytes / 1024, color = implementation)) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.6), size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~N) + scale_y_log10() + theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(x = "Batch size", y = "Recorded allocation per 15-epoch run (KiB; log scale)",
       subtitle = "Only positive recorded allocations shown; missing points listed below")
allocation_plot
```

```{r}
#| label: sgd-unrecorded-allocation
# Explicitly identify missing points without claiming zero memory usage.
knitr::kable(unrecorded[, c("N", "batch", "implementation", "allocation")],
             row.names = FALSE)
```

R's tracker does not capture all small allocations or native C++ memory.
**No allocation recorded** does not mean no memory use. Small batches may appear
to allocate less simply because the profiler misses their small temporary objects.
Use this plot to describe recorded allocations only; use the process-memory plot
below for a measurement including the whole R session. Matching final MSE is checked
between R and C++ at each batch size, but different batch sizes need not reach the
same accuracy under this common epoch budget and learning-rate schedule.

## Peak memory in separate R sessions

To include memory outside R's allocation tracker, measure maximum resident process
memory using macOS's `/usr/bin/time -l`. Each measurement starts a fresh R session.
Both sessions load the same code and Rcpp library and read the same precomputed
input. Compilation happens beforehand and is cached. Startup, library loading,
input storage and the solver all contribute to the process peak, so these are
**total session peaks**, not isolated gradient allocations. Five repetitions help
show measurement variability; small differences should not be overinterpreted.
The same four batch sizes are measured at N = 15,000.

```{r}
#| label: sgd-process-memory
# This measurement uses the macOS utility available on this project computer.
# Keeping it separate from bench::mark avoids confusing peak memory with allocation.
peak_memory <- data.frame()
if (Sys.info()[["sysname"]] == "Darwin") {
  cache <- tempfile("sgd-cpp-cache-")
  dir.create(cache)
  cpp_file <- normalizePath("project_B/gradient.cpp")
  Rcpp::sourceCpp(cpp_file, cacheDir = cache)
  input_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
  worker <- tempfile(fileext = ".R")
  # Both child processes receive exactly the same data and setup.
  saveRDS(list(problem = p, start = start, orders = orders, rates = rates,
               model = normalizePath("project_B/model.R"),
               cpp = cpp_file, cache = cache), input_file)
  writeLines(c(
    'args <- commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE)',
    'input <- readRDS(args[1])',
    'source(input$model)',
    'Rcpp::sourceCpp(input$cpp, cacheDir = input$cache)',
    'batch <- as.integer(args[3])',
    'invisible(gc())'), worker)
  dump("dose_sgd_r", file = worker, append = TRUE)
  cat('\nif (args[2] == "R") {\n',
      '  fit <- dose_sgd_r(input$start, input$problem, input$orders, input$rates, batch)\n',
      '} else {\n',
      '  fit <- dose_sgd_cpp(input$start, input$problem$z, input$problem$y, input$orders, input$rates, batch)\n',
      '}\nstopifnot(all(is.finite(fit)))\n', file = worker, append = TRUE)
  for (batch in sgd_batch_sizes) {
  for (repetition in 1:5) {
    for (implementation in c("R", "Rcpp")) {
      output <- system2("/usr/bin/time", c("-l",
        shQuote(file.path(R.home("bin"), "Rscript")), shQuote(worker),
        shQuote(input_file), implementation, as.character(batch)), stdout = TRUE, stderr = TRUE)
      stopifnot(is.null(attr(output, "status")))
      line <- grep("maximum resident set size", output, value = TRUE)
      stopifnot(length(line) == 1)
      bytes <- as.numeric(strsplit(trimws(line), "[[:space:]]+")[[1]][1])
      peak_memory <- rbind(peak_memory, data.frame(implementation, batch,
        repetition, peak_MiB = bytes / 1024^2))
    }
  }
  }
  unlink(c(worker, input_file))
  unlink(cache, recursive = TRUE)
  knitr::kable(peak_memory, digits = 2)
} else {
  cat("Peak process-memory experiment requires macOS /usr/bin/time -l.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: sgd-process-memory-plot
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
if (nrow(peak_memory) > 0) {
  ggplot(peak_memory, aes(factor(batch), peak_MiB, color = implementation)) +
    ggbeeswarm::geom_quasirandom(width = 0.15, dodge.width = 0.6, size = 2.5) +
    stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "point", shape = 95, size = 9,
                 color = "black", position = position_dodge(width = 0.6),
                 aes(group = interaction(batch, implementation))) +
    expand_limits(y = 0) + theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
    labs(x = "Batch size", y = "Peak resident process memory (MiB)",
         subtitle = "N = 15,000; 15 epochs; separate R sessions with identical setup")
}
```

The C++ loop reuses four parameter values and scalar intermediates, whereas R
repeatedly constructs gradient intermediates. This can reduce runtime and memory
pressure, but does not guarantee a large reduction in total process peak: the R
runtime, libraries and input data may dominate. Report the measured differences,
including overlap, rather than claiming zero memory use or universal memory savings.

# Interpreting the combined experiments

Judge accuracy and runtime together. Starts and step sizes test sensitivity; geometry
shows how similar per-evaluation cost can require different optimization effort.
Deterministic momentum adds work and may restart, but can reduce the accepted updates
needed. Stochastic momentum can oscillate, and AdaGrad can damp later progress.
Full-batch scheduled GD takes far fewer updates under an equal-pass budget. These
observations do not establish a universal winner.

For repeated doses, exact compression can be more valuable than changing update
rules. Continuous doses lack this shortcut. This connects the experimental design,
numerical behavior and computational costs.
